What your own numbers actually mean

Every metric in your PP2 evaluation, explained from zero — what it measures, why you chose it over the alternatives, and the trap hiding inside it. Written to be read once tonight and skimmed again in the corridor.

00

The five-sentence version

If you remember nothing else, remember this shape. Everything in this document is one of these five sentences expanded.

1. Your module does not guess which sign someone made — it grades a sign you already asked them for.

2. It grades by measuring the distance between the learner's hand movement and a real signer's recording, using Dynamic Time Warping so signing slowly is not penalised.

3. To know whether that distance means anything, you checked whether it can tell a correct rendition apart from a different sign — on 557 recordings that label themselves.

4. It can, about three times in four: AUC 0.744. You always quote that next to the 65.4% baseline, because the test set has far more wrong-sign pairs than correct ones, and raw accuracy would flatter you.

5. That is not your proposal's "90% agreement with an expert" target. Nothing you have measured is. That target needs a teacher grading real learners, and that is the pilot.

Sentence 5 is the one that keeps you safe. A panel forgives a missing result. It does not forgive a proxy dressed up as the real thing.

01

The vocabulary

Each term below has three parts: what it means in plain words, what your number is, and the trap. The trap is what a panel member reaches for when they want to test whether you understand the metric or just copied it.

Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)

the measurement

A way of comparing two sequences that are the same shape but not the same speed. It stretches and squeezes time so that matching moments line up, then adds up how far apart they are once aligned.

Picture two people signing THANK_YOU, one slowly. Frame-by-frame subtraction would call them completely different, because at frame 20 one is finishing and the other is halfway. DTW slides them into alignment first. What is left over is genuine difference in the shape of the movement — which is what you want to grade.

It also gives you an alignment path: which of the learner's frames matched which reference frame. That is why you can say "your ring finger was too extended at this moment". A neural classifier would give you a label and a confidence, and neither can be turned into that sentence without inventing it.

The trap — "your project is called transformer-based, so why is your component not a transformer?" Answer: because recognition and grading are different jobs. Recognition is Lahiru's component and it is learned. Grading a known sign needs localisable error and needs no per-sign training data — and labelled learner attempts, which a learned grader would need, do not exist for SSL yet. That is what the pilot starts producing.

Normalised distance

the units

One number for "how different were these two hand movements". Zero means identical. Bigger means more different. It has no upper limit and no natural good/bad line.

Normalised means two nuisances were divided out before comparing: every landmark is measured relative to the wrist (so standing left or right of frame changes nothing) and scaled by hand size (so standing closer to the camera changes nothing). The units are "hand-size units", which is why the x-axis of your distribution chart says that.

Your numbersTwo takes of the same sign typically sit 0.458 apart. The closest pair of genuinely different signs sits 0.135 apart.
The trap — a distance is not a probability and not a score. Everything downstream — the 0–100 score, the threshold, the AUC — is something you fitted on top of this number. Say "fitted", never "chosen".

Positive and negative pairs

the ground truth

To test whether the distance means anything, you need examples of "this is right" and "this is wrong". Your corpus gives you both for free.

Positive pair = two takes of the same sign by the same signer. That is what a correct rendition looks like, performed twice. You have 524.
Negative pair = a take of one sign against a take of a different sign. That is what performing the wrong sign looks like. You have 992.

The corpus holds 557 takes over 33 signs, but only 32 of those signs are usable — one has a single take, so it cannot form a positive pair. That is why your charts say 32 signs / 557 takes: if someone asks why the two numbers differ, that is the whole answer.

No human sat down and annotated anything. The corpus labels itself, because it already records which sign each clip is. This is the single most defensible thing about your evaluation — there is no room for you to have graded your own homework.

The trap — "so a positive pair is a learner attempt?" No. It is a fluent signer performing correctly, twice. That means you measured the natural variation of a correct rendition, which is narrower than a learner's would be — so every constant you fitted is optimistic. Say that before they say it. It is printed on your generated report already.

Threshold

evaluation device only

A line drawn across the distance axis. Below the line, call it "same sign"; above it, call it "different". Move the line and you get different behaviour.

Your best line sits at distance 0.370, where you get the highest raw accuracy: 74.6%.

The trap — your product never applies a threshold. There is no yes/no decision anywhere in the shipped app. The threshold exists only so you can put a number on how separable the two groups are. If you let a panel believe the product classifies, every hard question after that lands harder than it should.

TPR and FPR

what a threshold costs

Two rates that describe what one threshold does, from the two sides.

TPR — true positive rate, also called recall or sensitivity. Of all the pairs that really are the same sign, what fraction did you call "same"? Yours at the best-accuracy threshold: 0.357.
FPR — false positive rate. Of all the pairs that really are different signs, what fraction did you wrongly call "same"? Yours: 0.048.

Read them together and the picture is honest: the "best" threshold is a cautious one. It says "different sign" most of the time. It misses two-thirds of correct renditions, and in exchange it almost never mistakes a wrong sign for a right one.

The trap — if you only quote accuracy, TPR 0.357 is exactly the number a sharp panellist will dig out and use. Volunteer it. "The optimum buys its accuracy by rejecting — which is what an imbalanced set rewards, and it is one more reason we don't ship a threshold."

ROC curve

every threshold at once

Slide the threshold from one end of the distance axis to the other. At each stop, plot the pair (FPR, TPR) as a point. Join the points and you have the ROC curve.

The diagonal line is a coin flip: any point on it means your TPR and FPR rise together, which is what random guessing does. The further the curve bulges up and to the left, the better the distance separates the two groups at every threshold, not just a lucky one.

The trap — nothing on the ROC curve is your product's operating point, because your product has no operating point. The dot marked on your chart is the best-accuracy threshold, and it is there for reference only.

AUC — area under the ROC curve

your headline

One number summarising the whole ROC curve. 0.5 is a coin flip. 1.0 is perfect separation.

The definition worth memorising, because it is the one that makes sense out loud:

Pick one correct-rendition pair and one wrong-sign pair at random. AUC is the probability that the correct one gets the smaller distance.

So 0.744 means: about three times in four, your distance ranks the right thing as closer. Not brilliant. Not luck. Honest.

Why this is the headlineIt is threshold-free — you never had to choose a cut-off, so you cannot be accused of choosing a flattering one. And it is insensitive to class imbalance — 992 negatives against 524 positives does not move it. Those are the two attacks available on any accuracy figure, and AUC is immune to both.

Majority-class baseline

the comparison

The dumbest model imaginable: ignore the input entirely and always answer with whichever class is more common. Here that is "different sign", and it is right 992 / 1516 = 65.4% of the time.

This is the number that turns 74.6% from a grade into a measurement. On its own, 74.6% sounds like a weak pass. Against a baseline of 65.4% it is a gain of 9.2 points — modest, real, and stated by someone who knows what they are doing.

The trap — "74.6% compared to what?" is the single worst question to be caught by, because it makes the rest of your evaluation look unexamined. So you never say 74.6% without 65.4% in the same breath. Ever. fig9 exists purely so the slide says it for you.

Balanced accuracy

the imbalance made visible

Accuracy computed as if both classes were the same size: the average of how well you do on positives and how well you do on negatives — (TPR + (1 − FPR)) / 2.

Yours: (0.357 + 0.952) / 2 = 0.654, so 65.4%.

Watch this one — your balanced accuracy (65.4%) happens to land on the same number as your majority baseline (65.4%). They are different quantities that coincide. If a panellist points at the chart and says "two bars are identical", that is your answer — one is a dumb model's raw accuracy, the other is your scorer's imbalance-corrected accuracy, and it is a coincidence of this dataset. Knowing that cold is worth more than another decimal place anywhere else.

Median, p95, and why not the mean

latency

Sort every measurement smallest to largest. The median is the one in the middle. p95 is the value that 95% of measurements fall below — the "almost worst case".

A mean is the wrong tool for timings, because one unlucky run where the operating system was busy drags it upward and misrepresents the typical experience. The median says what usually happens; p95 says what happens on a bad day. Together they describe a distribution honestly; a mean alone does not.

Your numbersmedian 1.8 ms, p95 12.6 ms, max 21.5 ms, over n = 40 references, against a 300 ms budget.
The trap — this is the scoring stage only. It excludes hand-landmark inference, React's render commit and the browser's paint, and it ran in Node on a development machine, not in a participant's browser. If you let "1.8 ms" stand as the answer to the 300 ms target, you have overclaimed — and the correction, coming from them, is far more damaging than the qualifier coming from you.

Percentile anchors — how the 0–100 score was fitted

the score the learner sees

The learner never sees a distance. They see a score out of 100. That conversion needs two anchor points: a distance that means 100, and a distance that means 0.

You set them from measured data: D_PERFECT = 0.22 is the 10th percentile of correct renditions, and D_ZERO = 0.77 is the 90th percentile. In words: the best tenth of genuinely correct attempts score 100, and the worst tenth score 0. Everything between is interpolated.

Why this matters more than it soundsThe previous anchors were 0.05 and 0.35 — assumed before any data existed. 0.35 sat below the median correct rendition, which means a genuinely correct attempt was being shown a score of zero. Calibrating against data is what caught it. This is your best concrete before-and-after, and it proves the calibration was necessary rather than ceremonial.

Score gap

the operational metric

The difference between the average score a correct rendition receives and the average score a different sign receives. This is the only metric on this page that describes something a user actually experiences.

Your numberscorrect renditions average 56.7, different signs average 28.0 — a gap of 28.7 points. 60% of correct renditions score 50 or above, against 21% of different signs.

When someone asks "but what does 0.744 mean for a learner?", this is the answer. AUC characterises the metric; the score gap characterises the product.

02

Why accuracy lies — move the threshold yourself

Reading that "raw accuracy flatters under imbalance" is not the same as feeling it. Drag the threshold. Watch accuracy stay high while the scorer catches almost nothing.

0.370
Raw accuracy—
Baseline65.4%
Balanced accuracy—
TPR — correct caught—
FPR — wrong accepted—

What to notice. Push the threshold left and raw accuracy climbs toward the baseline — because saying "different sign" to everything is right 65.4% of the time here. Accuracy rewards you for refusing to commit. TPR is the column that tells the truth, and it collapses. That is the entire argument for leading with AUC.

This panel is a teaching illustration built from your class counts (524 / 992) and the shape of fig1. It is not a re-plot of your data and no number from it belongs in the report — the real ones are in raw-metrics.json.

04

The four proposal targets, and what "measured" means

One of four is measured. One has a proxy that measures something else and you say so. Two depend on the pilot. Knowing which is which, instantly, is worth more than any single number.

TargetStatusWhat exists — and what it is not
Feedback latency ≤ 300 ms Measured
scoring stage		 median 1.8 ms, p95 12.6 ms, n = 40. Not end-to-end: excludes landmark inference, React's commit and paint. End-to-end is instrumented in the app and needs ~20 real attempts before its p95 means anything.
Feedback accuracy ≥ 90% vs expert Not measured
proxy reported		 AUC 0.744, 74.6% against a 65.4% baseline. That measures can a correct rendition be told from a different sign — a different question from does the feedback agree with a teacher. Needs learner attempts graded by an SSL teacher.
Learning gain ≥ 20% over 10 sessions Instrumented
needs the pilot		 Every attempt carries a sessionId, so "after N sessions" is countable rather than inferred. Zero participants so far.
System Usability Scale ≥ 70 Not measured
needs the pilot		 SUS is a standard 10-item questionnaire scored 0–100; 68 is the conventional average and 70 is a mild "above average" bar. The instrument itself has not been prepared yet — no code needed, it simply does not exist.

One more thing to have ready: freeze the UI from the first participant. SUS scores a system — if P01 rates one build and P05 rates another, the mean describes nothing that exists. A mid-study UI change is also indistinguishable from learning, which would confound the learning-gain measurement. Participants get a pinned deployment URL, not the moving production alias.

05

The questions that will hurt

Not the factual ones — those are in DEFENCE.md. These are the ones designed to find out whether the person answering understands their own work.

“Walk me through how you got from a video to a score.”

Video → MediaPipe extracts 21 hand landmarks per frame → landmarks are made wrist-relative and divided by hand size → DTW aligns the learner's sequence against the reference and returns one distance → that distance is mapped onto 0–100 using two anchors fitted from data → the alignment path is walked back to find which joint deviated most and when, which becomes the written hint.

Why this one hurts: it is unanswerable if you only memorised results. Say it once out loud tonight and it will come out fine tomorrow.

“Your grid search found 78.6% and you shipped 74.2%. Explain.”

The search optimises "is this the same sign?" — a classification objective. The scorer's job is to grade a sign the learner was already asked for. The maximum sits at zero movement weight, and movement is a phonological parameter of SSL: a learner with the right handshape and the wrong movement has made a real error, and a scorer blind to movement would award them full marks. So we took the measured gain up to 0.8 and stopped.

This is the strongest single item you own — a documented case of declining a metric improvement because the metric was not the goal. If you get one open-ended "tell us about a design decision", tell this one.

“How do you know your reported numbers match your code?”

The reports are written by the tests that measure them and carry the line "Generated by … Do not edit by hand". The charts are plotted from a JSON export produced by the same scoreAttempt() the deployed app calls — the plotting script performs no measurement of its own. We re-ran the whole suite last night and git diff on the reports came back empty: not one character moved.

Then offer to run it. Repeatability is your strongest area and the panel asked for it by name — do not let it stay an assertion when it can be a demonstration.

“Has any Deaf person used or validated this?”

Not yet, and it is our most significant limitation. We have the partnership with the School for the Deaf, Ratmalana, and the plan is references recorded with a teacher there — which would also be the first references the app could present as authoritative rather than provisional. Right now we are a hearing team building from public corpora, and we have been careful not to invent vocabulary, glosses or sentence order anywhere in the system.

Answer it flat, with no hedging and no defensiveness. The "we invented nothing" clause is the part that shows the limitation was respected rather than merely noticed.

“What would you do differently?”

Start the pilot earlier. The build finished on schedule and the evaluation did not, because recruitment has lead time that nothing else can absorb. Second, record our own references with a signer sooner — reference quality bounds everything the scorer can do, and we found that out late.

A real answer with a cause and a consequence. "We'd add more features" is the answer that loses marks here.

06

Test yourself

Answer out loud before opening each one. If you can do ten out of ten without reading, you are done for tonight.

What does AUC 0.744 mean, in one sentence, without the word "area"?

Pick one correct-rendition pair and one wrong-sign pair at random; about three times in four, the correct one has the smaller distance.

Why is 74.6% not a good number to say on its own?

Because the test set is imbalanced 524 to 992, so a model that always answered "different sign" would score 65.4%. Alone, 74.6% sounds like a grade; against its baseline it is a gain of 9.2 points.

Your balanced accuracy and your baseline are both 65.4%. Is that a bug?

No — they are different quantities that coincide on this dataset. One is a dumb model's raw accuracy; the other is your scorer's accuracy corrected for imbalance.

Does your product apply a threshold?

No. There is no yes/no decision anywhere in the shipped app. The threshold exists only as an evaluation device for characterising the distance metric. What ships is the continuous 0–100 score.

Why DTW instead of a neural network?

Four reasons: it localises the error so a corrective hint is possible; it is speed-invariant by construction; it needs no per-sign training data, and labelled learner attempts do not exist for SSL yet; and it decouples this component from the recognition model. Concede cleanly that a learned scorer is the obvious successor once expert-graded attempts exist.

Where do 0.22 and 0.77 come from?

They are the 10th and 90th percentiles of the measured correct-rendition distance distribution — so the best tenth of correct attempts score 100 and the worst tenth score 0. The previous values were assumed, and one of them put a genuinely correct attempt at zero.

Is 1.8 ms your feedback latency?

No. It is the scoring stage only, in Node, on a development machine. It excludes landmark inference, React's commit and the browser's paint. The end-to-end figure is instrumented in the app and needs about 20 real attempts before its p95 is meaningful.

What is your ground truth, and what is it not?

The corpus labels itself: two takes of one sign are a correct rendition twice, takes of different signs are a wrong-sign attempt. It is not expert judgment of learner attempts, which is what the ≥90% target requires and what the pilot will produce.

Why is non-manual marker scoring missing, and what happened to its 10%?

The build tracks hand landmarks only, so facial expression, head tilt and body movement are not captured — reporting a number for them would be fabricating one. The 10% was reallocated to accuracy, giving 50 / 30 / 20, and the deviation is documented in the source, the README and the app's own UI.

Someone asks you to reproduce a figure right now. What do you do?

Run the test suite, run the evaluation export with EVAL_EXPORT=1, run make_figures.py, then git diff the reports to show nothing moved. About twenty seconds. Volunteer the caveat first: the calibration takes are gitignored derived data, so on a fresh clone those tests skip silently rather than fail — check the corpus count printed in calibration-report.md.
